explanation: Fires on function words and conjunctions (or, but, not, and, on, ':', ',') at points of contrast or alternatives, especially in license or disclaimer boilerplate ('Dual License: MIT or GPL', 'Software or, alternatively', 'those of the writer and not'). It also picks up odd tokens in other contexts, so it does not follow one clean rule.

Fires on words that open or connect the items of an inclusive enumeration or range: 'both' in 'both X and Y', 'as' in 'as diverse as', 'all' in 'of all sizes', 'particularly'/'especially'/'INCLUDING' introducing examples, and the 'and'/'or' before the last item of a list. It is strongest on 'both'/'all'/'as' that introduce the span, and moderate on list-final 'and'.

Fires on a wide range of unrelated tokens (verbs like 'trying'/'transform', nouns like 'post'/'body', digits in URLs and dates, 'you', code tokens such as 'new' or '$cmd'), with no clear shared token identity or context.

Fires on tokens near the very start of a document or right after a heading or title: the first function word or punctuation after a name or title ('21st Infantry Regiment (', 'Kampschroeder was born', '2007 to be hottest', 'Wer dumm fragt,'). Position early in a short header-like line seems to matter more than the token's identity.

Fires on a digit in the second position of a multi-digit number, i.e. the digit right after the leading digit (2[2]9, -3[0]6, 4[1]:660, 5,[2]10). It is strongest in counts, measurements, citations and patent numbers, and weaker for years, timestamps and decimals.

Fires on the second element of a repeated or paired structure: mainly the ' [@' that opens the second citation in a list like '[@bib1], [@bib2]', and the second year in ranges such as '1984-85' or '1910–13'. It is weaker on repeated code lines such as a second 'import' or '#include'.

Fires on mid-word continuation tokens and on punctuation or function words in code and technical text (UITransition[Context], intramus[cular]ly, acetal[dehyde], '(int)', commas in argument lists), with no evident unifying semantics.

Fires inside names of space agencies and scientific research organisations, most strongly on 'Space'/'Station'/'Spacecraft'/'mission' in NASA/ESA contexts. It fires moderately on 'Research'/'Energy'/'Defense' in institution names (European Research Council, Atomic Energy) and on general research or capability words.

Fires on interior subword pieces of foreign-language words (German, Finnish, Swedish, Czech, Spanish, Italian) and of uncommon technical or legal words split into fragments (SUP[RE]ME, THIR[TE]ENTH, front[ot]emporal, pacl[it]axel), plus foreign function words inside proper names ('für', 'del', 'und'). The common factor is low-frequency, multi-token words.

Fires on a mixture: the space between the reporter series and the page number in legal citations ('F.3d 1420'), thousands-separator commas, word fragments in names ('Tr[out]beck', 'Super[power]'), and miscellaneous function words. There is no single coherent theme.

Fires on the name token right after 'class' (or 'module'/'namespace'/'type'/'@interface') in a code declaration, especially the second CamelCase part of the class name (DescribeDrdsComponents[Request], Email[Settings]Service). It fires weakly on section headings at line start in prose ('Introduction', 'Tags').

Fires on a mix: empty parentheses '()' after function names in code or error messages, 'not'/'n't' in emphatic negations, the second letter or letters of acronyms (PD[GF], H[A]), and assorted other tokens. No coherent single role.

Fires on structural or boundary tokens across very different contexts: 'v.' in case captions, '.' inside IP addresses, '://' in URLs, 'at'/'in' in stack traces, word fragments (pin-cush[ion], FD[MA]), commas in parentheticals. No clear unifying feature.

Fires on the first token of a placeholder, field name or description slot in code, config or forms: the first word of a JSDoc parameter description ('- The URL'), a quoted key ('"AWS"'), SQL column names, and 'your'/'their' in form-filling phrases ('Enter your email', 'contain your User ID'). It refers to what fills a named slot.

Fires on verbs or function words right after a subject that begin a predicate, especially light verbs 'take/took/taking', 'go/goes', 'pay' ('banned from taking part', 'took a 21-18 lead'). It also fires on other prepositions and miscellany, so it is only loosely coherent.

Fires on the second element of a contrastive or compound term pair, especially prefix-like tokens before a hyphen ('HLA' in HLA-class/HLA-DR, 'off'/'non' in 'on- or off-resonant', 'non-minority'), and on adjectives or determiners before a noun under contrast ('dry granules', 'a right lesion'). It also fires on unrelated code tokens.

Fires on the first or early subword fragment of a word that is split into several tokens, mostly in non-English (Portuguese, Czech, French, German, Slovenian, Japanese romaji) or all-caps text (PMDB[-R]J, spol[up]ráci, T[AC]OMA, [ ASS]AULT). It is strongest where the word continues after the token.

Fires on the name token in a function, method or constructor definition, i.e. the identifier right after 'function', 'def', 'public', a return type or 'class Name {' (Phone[book](), def [fit], function timeout[_init]). It fires weakly on other identifiers in code.

Fires on assorted tokens inside numbers, scores, citations and technical terms (score hyphens '2-2', 'N.E.2d', URL digits, 'Light' in sensor names, mid-word fragments), plus some ordinary words. No clear unifying rule.

Fires mainly on the end of a quote or sentence followed by a paragraph break ('."

', '?
', ').
'), especially right after quoted speech in news, and on the '9' of '19xx' years in court-case dates. It also fires on scattered tokens such as 'No you'.

Fires on tokens in PHP code and PHP ecosystem text: namespace backslashes, 'Psr', '__construct', 'use', paths like 'php/php5.4', PHP error messages ('Uncaught exception'), and mentions of PHP/Magento/Laravel. The PHP context matters more than the specific token.
